design_detail: Cross-sectional chemical analysis of purchased cannabis, filed as cross-sectional because each sample was analysed once. Two popular cultivars, Amnesia (described as Sativa-dominant) and White Widow (described as Indica-dominant), were bought as 1-gram samples at ten coffee shops in four Dutch cities on two visits about two months apart (18 Amnesia and 17 White Widow samples), and three pharmaceutical-grade varieties (Bedrocan, Bedrobinol, Bedica) were obtained from the official Dutch grower, Bedrocan BV, one batch each analysed in triplicate. Twenty-eight terpenoids and cannabinoids present at 0.5 mg/g or more were quantified by gas chromatography with flame-ionization detection in one laboratory and compared by principal component analysis (PCA). Three coffee-shop samples whose chemistry matched the other cultivar were excluded as presumed mix-ups. No people were studied and no effects were measured.
can_establish: That, in this small set of Dutch coffee-shop purchases around 2011, samples sold as Amnesia and as White Widow differed in terpenoids and minor cannabinoids but not in THC, that the chemistry of samples bought under the same name varied considerably, and that a few samples bought under one name matched the other.
cannot_establish: Whether Indica and Sativa labels track chemistry in general (two cultivars only, chosen for availability rather than as typical types); whether either cultivar or its chemistry produces different effects (none measured); how often products in shops are mislabelled (three post hoc exclusions in 35 samples from ten shops); or whether coffee-shop products vary more than pharmacy batches (the pharmacy figures are repeat analyses of one batch).

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people. One gram of each cultivar bought at ten coffee shops in Amsterdam, Utrecht, Groningen and Maastricht, each shop visited a second time about two months later to obtain different batches; samples came in the shops' small zip-lock bags (PDF p. 2). Three pharmaceutical-grade varieties supplied directly by the official Dutch grower, Bedrocan BV, grown from clones under standardized indoor conditions and quality-controlled (PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Amnesia and White Widow were chosen because both were generally available at all locations throughout the year (PDF p. 2); the authors had intended to include typical 'pure' Sativa and Indica strains but found none available in all ten shops (PDF p. 7). Compounds were analysed if present at a mean of at least 0.5 mg/g in at least one variety: 28 compounds (PDF pp. 3–4). Three samples whose chemistry matched the other cultivar were left out of the final evaluation (PDF pp. 5–6). The pharmacy variety Bediol (7.5% CBD) was not included (PDF p. 7).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (no people). Purchase dates are not given beyond two visits about two months apart; the paper was received in November 2011.
sample.attrition: Of 40 planned purchases, 5 were unavailable (2 Amnesia, 3 White Widow); of the 35 bought, 3 were excluded after analysis (PDF p. 4; PDF p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: Two popular cultivars from ten coffee shops (how the shops were chosen is not described) in one country, chosen for availability rather than as representative Sativa or Indica types. The three chemically discordant samples were excluded on the basis of the chemistry itself, which makes the two cultivars look more distinct and less variable than what was actually bought; the authors concede these might have been genuine specimens (PDF p. 5). The comparison varieties came from the first author's employer.

exposure.measurement: Label: the name under which each sample was bought, and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website (Sensi Seed Bank), chosen as the reference from popular culture (PDF p. 7). Chemistry: ethanol extraction, gas chromatography with flame-ionization detection in one laboratory, peak identities confirmed by GC–MS; all terpenoids quantified against a γ-terpinene standard curve and all cannabinoids against a THC curve; results in mg per g of plant material, not corrected for water content (PDF p. 3; PDF p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (product chemistry; no human exposure).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (no people studied). The analogous limitation: compounds below 0.5 mg/g were not analysed, and one compound was not identified (it was assumed to be a cannabinoid and kept in the analysis) (PDF p. 4).

comparison.controls: The two coffee-shop cultivars were compared with each other, and both with three pharmaceutical-grade varieties grown under controlled conditions; the pharmacy data are triplicate analyses of a single batch of each variety (Fig 2 legend, PDF p. 6).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to people. Unknown for the coffee-shop samples: genetics, growers, growing, drying, processing and storage conditions, and product age; the authors note that differences between coffee shops or their suppliers could cause chemical variation (PDF p. 7).

outcomes.instruments: GC-FID quantification of 28 compounds (terpenoids and cannabinoids); PCA (SIMCA-P+ 12.0, unit-variance scaling) shown as a scatter plot of the first two components with its loading plot; mean, standard deviation and relative standard deviation (RSD) of each compound per cultivar (Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 4–5; Fig 2, PDF p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Quantifying every terpenoid against one terpenoid standard and every cannabinoid against THC gives approximate concentrations; the authors accept small deviations from actual values and cite their earlier validation (PDF p. 4). The solid ellipse in Fig 2 is a 95% region for the whole data set; the dotted group ellipses were drawn by the authors as visual aids and signify no statistical test (Fig 2 legend).
outcomes.operationalization: Cultivars count as chemically distinct if their samples form separate groups in the PCA plot; within-cultivar variability is the RSD of each compound across purchases.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests are reported, although the text calls some differences significant and one non-significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. Samples were marked directly after purchase, kept in their packaging, and extracted in groups of eight by two people checking each other (PDF p. 6).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only. THC: Amnesia 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88; 16.75%), White Widow 159.5 mg/g (SD 26.76; 15.95%), reported as not significantly different, with no test shown (Table 1, PDF p. 4; PDF p. 5); by the editors' calculation the 8 mg/g difference is about a third of the pooled SD. Myrcene 2.9 mg/g in White Widow vs 0.7 in Amnesia; α-pinene 1.1 vs 0.5; β-caryophyllene 1.2 vs 2.1; CBG 5.4 vs 12.5; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia and not detected in White Widow (Table 1). PCA: PC1 27.2% and PC2 17.0% of variance (together 44.2%), PC3 11.4% (PDF p. 5). RSD above 25% for 14 compounds among the coffee-shop samples (PDF p. 6). Pharmacy THC: Bedrocan 211.9, Bedrobinol 135.0, Bedica 174.5 mg/g, RSDs 3.1–3.7% (Table 2, PDF p. 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: No statistical test is reported for any comparison; the number of samples per cultivar behind the Table 1 means (after the three exclusions) is not stated; the three excluded samples are shown in Fig 2 but their values are not given.
analysis.power: Not addressed: 18 and 17 samples of two cultivars, and three pharmacy batches.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Samples bought as Amnesia (described as Sativa-dominant) and as White Widow (Indica-dominant) formed two groups in a PCA of 28 compounds, separated by terpenoids and minor cannabinoids, while their THC content was similar (167.5 vs 159.5 mg/g). Within each name, several compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases. Three of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other chemically, and 5 of 40 attempted purchases were unavailable. Of the pharmacy varieties, one bred from a Haze background with a large share of Sativa genes resembled the Indica-dominant White Widow.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the analysis identified the constituents that define distinct chemovar groups and shows the usefulness of PCA for classification (PDF p. 1); with two cultivars from one country, one laboratory and no validation set, this is a demonstration rather than a classification. The text reads 44.2% of variance explained by two components as a relatively high degree of confidence (PDF p. 5), which variance explained does not measure, and calls differences significant without tests. It speculates, without effect data, that Amnesia's lower α-pinene, described as an anticholinesterase that may reduce THC's short-term memory deficits, would be noteworthy if Amnesia does have stronger memory effects and that myrcene might underlie the sedation attributed to Indica types (PDF p. 4). The conclusion that 20% of coffee-shop visits (8/40) failed to deliver a reliable product counts the three excluded samples as mix-ups, which the authors elsewhere concede might be genuine specimens (PDF p. 5; PDF p. 7). The contrast in variability with pharmacy cannabis sets purchases from different batches against repeat analyses of one batch, and the statement that no pharmacy compound varied by more than 25% is contradicted by Table 2. The closing view that standardized, quality-controlled sources may be the safer choice for people who use cannabis as a medicine comes from a first author employed by that standardized producer (PDF p. 7).

timeline.event: Same group: cultivars grown by clonal propagation under controlled conditions could be told apart by cannabinoid and terpenoid content, with reproducible profiles across batches (Fischedick et al., 2010, as described in this paper, PDF p. 7).
This study: two coffee-shop cultivars differ in terpenoids and minor cannabinoids, not in THC; considerable variation within each name.

Same first author, larger metabolomics follow-up ('From cultivar to chemovar II'): specific terpenes more often found in Indica- than Sativa-labelled samples (Hazekamp et al., 2016, as described by Smith et al., 2022).
89,923 compliance-tested US flower samples: the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category tied to strain names barely separates terpene profiles, while strain names are moderately consistent

replication.where_it_stands: Later and much larger datasets support the general point that terpene profiles, rather than THC, distinguish products sold under different names, and that the Indica/Sativa/Hybrid categories track that chemistry poorly (Smith et al., 2022). The specific Amnesia–White Widow contrast, the 20% figure for unreliable purchases and the variability comparison with pharmacy cannabis rest on this one small study.

funding.declared_conflicts: Disclaimer: A.H. has been employed by Bedrocan BV as head of Research and Development since February 2011 (PDF p. 7). No other statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Bedrocan BV, the first author's employer and the correspondence address, is the official Dutch grower that supplied the three pharmacy varieties compared here, and the paper concludes that products from a standardized, quality-controlled source may be the safer choice for people who use cannabis as a medicine (PDF p. 7). The second author was at the Natural Products Laboratory, Leiden University (PDF p. 1). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated purchases of many products sold under the same names and Indica/Sativa labels across shops, regions and time, analysed blind to the label in an accredited laboratory with compound-specific standards and a pre-specified statistical test of the label groups, without post hoc exclusions; and a blinded crossover study in people who use cannabis testing whether chemically distinct products with equal THC differ in effects.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Ten coffee shops in four Dutch cities fit the question of what a buyer got under two popular names in the Netherlands around 2011; they cannot stand for cannabis labelled Sativa or Indica in general.
How the ten shops were chosen is not stated; the two cultivars were chosen for availability; two purchases per shop and cultivar.
35 samples of two cultivars and three pharmacy batches.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Cities, number of shops and visits, packaging and analysis are described; purchase dates and shop selection are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Three of 35 samples were excluded after analysis because their chemistry matched the other cultivar, removing exactly the cases that bear on how reliable the names are.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: GC-FID with GC–MS confirmation, but all terpenoids quantified against one standard and all cannabinoids against THC, without correction for water content; the Sativa/Indica attribution comes from a seed company's website.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One laboratory and one method for all samples; extraction checked by two people.

No statistical tests although differences are called significant; variance explained by the PCA is read as confidence; between-batch purchase variability is compared with repeat analyses of one pharmacy batch.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Purchases, not respondents; unavailable products are reported (5 of 40).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The JBI prevalence checklist fits a descriptive cross-sectional analysis of purchased products; no instrument is designed for label-validity analyses of product chemistry. A small, unsystematic sample of two cultivars, the post hoc exclusion of chemically discordant samples, the absence of any statistical test and a conflict of interest bearing on the coffee-shop-versus-pharmacy comparison put the study at high risk of bias for any general claim. Citable as an early demonstration that two products sold under different popular names in Dutch coffee shops differed in terpenoids and minor cannabinoids but not in THC, and that products bought under one name varied considerably; not for how Indica and Sativa labels perform in general, not for mislabelling rates, and not for effects.

key_findings.finding: Samples: ten coffee shops in Amsterdam, Utrecht, Groningen and Maastricht, each visited twice about two months apart; 1 g each of Amnesia (described as a Sativa-dominant type) and White Widow (an Indica-dominant type) per visit. Of 40 planned purchases, 5 were unavailable (2 Amnesia, 3 White Widow), leaving 18 Amnesia and 17 White Widow samples; 28 compounds were present at a mean of 0.5 mg/g or more.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Sample collection, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Results and discussion › Sampling and analysis, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: THC content was similar in the two cultivars: Amnesia 167.5 mg/g (16.75%, SD 21.88) and White Widow 159.5 mg/g (15.95%, SD 26.76), which the authors report as not significantly different, giving no basis for telling the two apart by THC.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, row 26 (PDF p. 4); Results and discussion › PCA and quantitative analysis of coffee shop samples, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: No test statistic is reported. By the editors' calculation the 8 mg/g difference is about a third of the pooled SD.

key_findings.finding: The two cultivars differed in terpenoids and minor cannabinoids: White Widow had more myrcene (2.9 vs 0.7 mg/g, more than four times) and α-pinene (1.1 vs 0.5 mg/g), and contained guaiol, γ-eudesmol and β-eudesmol not detected in Amnesia; Amnesia had terpinolene (1.9 mg/g) and cis-ocimene (0.7 mg/g) not detected in White Widow, and more β-caryophyllene (2.1 vs 1.2 mg/g), CBC (2.8 vs 1.8) and CBG (12.5 vs 5.4).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (PDF p. 4); Results and discussion › Sampling and analysis, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 4); PCA and quantitative analysis of coffee shop samples, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: α-Guaiene (named as characteristic of Amnesia) and α-bisabolol (named as characteristic of White Widow) were each detected in only one sample (Table 1, asterisks).

key_findings.finding: In the PCA, Amnesia and White Widow samples formed two separate groups; the first two components explained 27.2% and 17.0% of the variance (44.2% together) and the third another 11.4%. Monoterpenoids, sesquiterpenoids and minor cannabinoids distinguished the cultivars.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › PCA and quantitative analysis of coffee shop samples, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 5); Fig 2a–b (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Three of the samples bought (18 + 17) had the chemical profile of the other cultivar; the authors assumed mix-ups at the coffee shop and left them out of the final evaluation, while conceding they might have been genuine specimens of the requested cultivars, which would make the variation within each cultivar even larger.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › PCA and quantitative analysis of coffee shop samples, 4th paragraph (begins PDF p. 5, continues PDF p. 6); Fig 2 legend (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: The text and the figure legend disagree on which way the mix-ups went (see reporting issues); the plot agrees with the legend.

key_findings.finding: Chemical variability within each cultivar was considerable: relative standard deviations above 25% were found for 14 compounds, for example myrcene 39.5% and CBG 43.2% in White Widow and terpinolene 39.6% in Amnesia; THC varied with RSDs of 16.8% (White Widow) and 13.1% (Amnesia).
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › PCA and quantitative analysis of coffee shop samples, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 6); Table 1 (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 1: RSD above 25% in 14 compound–cultivar pairs (8 in White Widow, 6 in Amnesia, counting the misaligned γ-selinene value as Amnesia's RSD), which is 13 distinct compounds because β-caryophyllene exceeds 25% in both.

key_findings.finding: Pharmacy varieties: Bedica, derived from an Indica type, closely resembled White Widow, which the authors say would explain their similarity; Bedrobinol, bred from a Haze variety with a large share of Sativa genes, also resembled White Widow, which they call surprising and suggest may reflect its very low terpene content; Bedrocan, from a Jack Herer background described as slightly Sativa-dominant, resembled neither coffee-shop type nor the other pharmacy varieties and lay closer to Amnesia, with myrcene, cis-ocimene and terpinolene at least twice Amnesia's levels. [The lead 'Lineage labels did not predict the pharmacy varieties' chemistry' goes beyond the source: the authors present Bedica and Bedrocan as consistent with their lineage; only Bedrobinol was unexpected.]
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Comparing coffee shop to pharmacy samples, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig 2a

key_findings.finding: The pharmacy varieties were analysed as triplicates of one batch each; the authors state that no pharmacy compound varied by more than 25%, cite their earlier study's RSDs of about 7.6% for cannabinoids and 11.0% for terpenoids (Bedrocan) and 5.5% and 4.3% (Bedica), and note that Dutch medicinal cannabis is allowed up to 15% variation in THC and CBD.
key_findings.locator: Results and discussion › Comparing coffee shop to pharmacy samples, 1st and 4th paragraphs (4th begins PDF p. 6, continues PDF p. 7); Fig 2 legend (PDF p. 6)
key_findings.note: Contradicted in part by Table 2 (PDF p. 5): Bedica β-pinene has an RSD of 86.7% (mean 0.3 mg/g, SD 0.28). Triplicate analyses of one batch measure analytical repeatability, not batch-to-batch variation.

key_findings.finding: Counting the 5 unavailable products and the 3 presumed mix-ups, the authors estimate that, if their experience is representative, in 20% of cases (8 of 40 visits) a buyer would not receive a reliable service at an average coffee shop. [Source says 'reliable service'; five of the eight were unavailability, not a product.]

The Sativa or Indica background of each cultivar was taken from a seed company's website (Sensi Seed Bank); the authors had intended to include typical 'pure' Sativa and Indica strains but could not find any that were available in all ten coffee shops.

The authors summarize popular descriptions of Sativa effects (uplifting, energetic, cerebral) and Indica effects (body relaxation, sleep, 'couchlock'), drawn from a popular book, and state that whether such subjective descriptions relate to the morphological Indica–Sativa distinction or to any chemical classification had not been properly confirmed.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Bridging the gap between culture and science, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The text says two samples bought as White Widow resembled Amnesia and one Amnesia sample the reverse (PDF p. 5), while the Fig 2 legend says two samples bought as Amnesia resembled White Widow and one the reverse (PDF p. 6); the plot itself shows two closed triangles (bought as Amnesia) inside the White Widow group and one closed circle inside the Amnesia group, agreeing with the legend.
reporting_issues.consequence: The running text appears to have the direction reversed; the count of three discordant samples is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that no component of the pharmacy varieties varied by more than 25% (PDF pp. 6–7) is contradicted by Table 2, where Bedica β-pinene has a mean of 0.3 mg/g, SD 0.28 and RSD 86.7% (PDF p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the main finding, but the contrast between pharmacy and coffee-shop variability is overstated.

The comparison mixes analytical repeatability with batch-to-batch variation and favours the pharmacy products; the earlier study's RSDs are also described as coming from 'a standard batch' of each variety, so they too may reflect within-batch rather than between-batch variation (that study was not read).

reporting_issues.issue: Table rows are misaligned: in Table 1 the γ-selinene values sit in the wrong columns (White Widow SD 0.7 and RSD 0.25; Amnesia SD 34.6), presumably meaning an Amnesia mean of 0.7 mg/g, SD 0.25 and RSD 34.6%; in Table 2 the CBD values for Bedrobinol and Bedica are similarly shifted. γ-Selinene and δ-guaiene share the same relative retention time (1.136).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; values in these rows must be read with care, and the γ-selinene reading affects the count of compounds above 25% RSD.

reporting_issues.issue: Compounds presented as characterizing a cultivar were detected in a single sample: α-guaiene in Amnesia and α-bisabolol in White Widow (Table 1 asterisks), as were terpineol and CBGM in White Widow.
reporting_issues.consequence: These compounds cannot be said to characterize either cultivar.

reporting_issues.issue: Differences are called significant (myrcene and α-pinene in White Widow; Bedrocan outside the 95% ellipse) and THC is called not significantly different, but no statistical test is reported, and the number of samples per cultivar after the three exclusions is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: All comparisons are descriptive; none of the stated significances can be checked.
